newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. worried about arms surveillance in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.N. worried about arms surveillance in Iraq.

text.p: Iraq and the United Nations appear to be headed for a standoff on arms surveillance programmes, with the chief U.N. inspector warning President Saddam Hussein to stop obstructing his work.

In a major half-year report to the Security Council on Friday, Rolf Ekeus, head of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of Iraqi disarmament, said Iraq's leadership had to make a political decision "once and for all" on its ambitions to retain and acquire dangerous arms.

At issue are obstacles Iraq has allegedly put in the way of a long-term monitoring system set up to ensure Baghdad does not rebuild its arms machine, which is nearly but not entirely dismantled six years after the Gulf War.

The Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), responsible for nuclear materials, in a separate report by its director Hans Blix, said that Iraqi obstruction "makes it impossible to consider the ongoing monitoring and vertification plan to be fully operational."
Diplomats close to the operation said that Iraq's attempts to limit the monitoring were serious and might be the next major confrontation between the two sides.
U.N. inspectors foresee an expansion of the surveillance as Iraq begins to recover from sanctions by a limited easing of the oil embargo.

A clean bill of health by Ekeus, head of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of ridding Iraq of weapons of mass destruction, is a key requirement before the embargo on Iraqi oil exports can be lifted entirely. Iraq has been under U.N. sanctions since its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.
Iraq's foreign minister, Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf, is expected to arrive in New York late on Monday and then spend most of the week talking to Security Council members privately about the report.

Ekeus, in his report, said a solution to the difficulties "requires a major political decision by Iraq's leadership to give up, once and for all, all capabilities and ambition to retain or acquire the proscribed weapons," he said.

Iraq, he said, on repeated occasions threatened to shoot down helicopters used by the commission if they did not follow certain routes. At times Iraqi helicopters had flown dangerously close and Iraq personnel on board "have attempted to wrest control of the aircraft."

Another example of obstruction was Iraq's National Monitoring Directorate (NMD), which acts as a liaison for the inspectors. "When minders from the NMD escort the commmission's inspectors, they have often interrupted interviews and instructed Iraqi site personnel to provide wrong information or to refuse to answer relevant questions," Ekeus said.

But Ekeus, who will be leaving his job before September to become Sweden's ambassador to Washington, said little remained unknown about Baghdad's nuclear, biological, chemical and ballistic missile potential, but what was unknown could still cause devastating damage and casualties.

If a single missile warhead were filled with anthrax, an infectious animal disease that can spread to humans, "millions of lethal doses could be spread in an attack on any city of the region," he said.

Little progress was made in reporting the whereabouts of such biological warfare agents as aflatoxin, associated with fungal contaminated food grains and known for inducing liver cancer. The report said Iraq's declarations on destruction of the agent was not supported by sufficient evidence.
